extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in an introductory proof-based mathematics course (sets and logic)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook material presenting definitions, principles, examples, and exercises on sets, indexed collections, number-systems-as-sets, Russell's paradox, and propositional logic (statements, connectives, truth tables). Intended to teach how to reason and write proofs using these notions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of indexed sets and unions/intersections
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an indexed family of sets A_α (α ∈ I) express and interpret unions and intersections. Example: if A_α = [1,2] × {α} for α ∈ [0,2], then the union over α is [1,2] × [0,2] (and the corresponding intersection statements follow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualize members of the family as slices or fibers; unions collect all slices, intersections pick common points. Use examples (rectangles, vertical planes) to compute unions and intersections explicitly. The text demonstrates rewriting the indexed expressions as Cartesian products to simplify computing unions/intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometry of parameterized families (planes P(a,b))
rubrics_metrics.description: For (a,b) ∈ R^2 define P(a,b) = {(x,y,z) ∈ R^3 : a x + b y = 0}. Each P(a,b) (with (a,b) ≠ (0,0)) is a vertical plane through the z-axis; P(0,0)=R^3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe that every P(a,b) contains the z-axis, so the intersection of all such P(a,b) is the z-axis. Conversely, any (a,b,c) ∈ R^3 belongs to some P(a,b) (e.g. P(−b,a)), so the union of all P(a,b) is R^3. Use such geometric observations to compute unions/intersections of parametrized families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-ordering principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Any non-empty subset of the positive integers N has a smallest element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept this as a basic principle for proofs involving integers (used often without justification). It is the basis for proofs like the division algorithm. The book notes the corresponding statement is false for R>0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division Algorithm (Fact 1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given integers a and b with b > 0, there exist integers q and r for which a = q b + r and 0 ≤ r < b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the well-ordering principle: consider A = {a − x b : x ∈ Z, 0 ≤ a − x b} and pick its smallest element r = a − q b. Show 0 ≤ r < b by contradiction (if r ≥ b then r − b ∈ A is smaller). This algorithmic decomposition into quotient and remainder is a standard tool in integer proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number systems as sets (von Neumann construction sketch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural numbers can be represented as sets: 0 = ∅, 1 = {0}, 2 = {0,1}, 3 = {0,1,2}, and in general n = {0,1,...,n−1}. Similarly other number systems can be built from sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states we will not develop this fully here but notes that arithmetic operations and number-systems can be defined set-theoretically; this is background justifying that mathematics can be described in set language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Russell's paradox and its resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Define A = { X : X is a set and X ∉ X }. Asking whether A ∈ A leads to a contradiction (A ∈ A iff A ∉ A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this paradox to motivate care in set formation; resolution comes from adopting axiomatic set theory (Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms) including the axiom of foundation which forbids infinitely descending membership chains or sets that contain themselves. The paradox shows precision in set-theoretic language is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: correct logic versus correct information
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is a process of deducing information correctly; correctness of the deduction is independent of the truth of premises. Example: deductive steps can be valid even if premises (e.g., 'Circle X has radius 3') are false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving theorems, apply logic to premises considered true; but conceptually distinguish validity (form) from truth of premises. This matters when exploring consequences of false assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement is a sentence or mathematical expression that is either definitely true or definitely false (has a definite truth value).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that sentences whose truth depends on unspecified variables (open sentences) are not statements. Examples and non-examples are given; use letters P,Q,R to denote statements for abstraction in logical manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open sentences and statements with variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that contain variables (e.g., Q(x): 'x is even') are open sentences and are not statements until variables are instantiated; we sometimes denote them P(x), P(x,y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat open sentences differently from statements; when variables are bound or quantified they can become statements. The book emphasizes notation and examples (e.g., P(x): 'if x is multiple of 6 then x is even').

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunction (P ∧ Q) truth table
rubrics_metrics.description: If P and Q are statements, P ∧ Q ('P and Q') is true exactly when both P and Q are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table: TT → T; TF, FT, FF → F. Use conjunction to build compound assertions; examples show checking truth in concrete numeric cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disjunction (P ∨ Q) truth table and inclusive 'or'
rubrics_metrics.description: P ∨ Q ('P or Q') is true when at least one of P or Q is true (inclusive-or).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table: TT, TF, FT → T; FF → F. Emphasize that mathematical 'or' is inclusive: 'one or both'. To express exclusive or use constructions like 'P or Q, but not both.' Examples contrast everyday language usage with the mathematical meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation (∼P) truth table and expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: ∼P ('It is not true that P') is true when P is false and false when P is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table: P true → ∼P false; P false → ∼P true. Give several English paraphrases of negation (e.g., 'It is false that P', 'P is not true'). Apply negation to statements and open sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional statements (P ⇒ Q) meaning and truth table
rubrics_metrics.description: P ⇒ Q ('If P, then Q') asserts that whenever P is true Q must also be true. The only false case is P true and Q false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table: TT → T; TF → F; FT, FF → T. Explain via examples (professor's promise) why rows with P false are true (promise not broken). List equivalent English formulations: 'Q if P', 'Q whenever P', 'P is sufficient for Q', 'Q is necessary for P', 'P only if Q', etc. Stress careful wording and how necessity/sufficiency relate to the conditional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converse and difference between P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P
rubrics_metrics.description: The converse of P ⇒ Q is Q ⇒ P; they are logically independent in general and express different things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples (multiple of 6 ⇒ divisible by 2 is true; divisible by 2 ⇒ multiple of 6 is false) to illustrate difference. Do not assume implication is reversible without proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional (P ⇔ Q) meaning and truth table
rubrics_metrics.description: P ⇔ Q is the conjunction (P ⇒ Q) ∧ (Q ⇒ P); it is true exactly when P and Q have the same truth value (both true or both false).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table: TT → T; FF → T; TF, FT → F. English equivalents: 'P if and only if Q', 'P is necessary and sufficient for Q'. Use to capture equivalence statements in definitions and theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building complex statements from connectives (e.g., exclusive or)
rubrics_metrics.description: More complex logical constructions are formed by combining ∧, ∨, ∼, ⇒, ⇔. For example, exclusive-or can be expressed as (P ∨ Q) ∧ ∼(P ∧ Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct truth tables for compound formulas by evaluating helper subexpressions. The textbook demonstrates computing such tables step-by-step and notes helper columns may be omitted once confident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translating English sentences into logical form
rubrics_metrics.description: Many English constructions correspond to logical forms; exercises convert sentences like 'A is invertible provided det(A) ≠ 0' into 'If P then Q' and 'necessary/sufficient' formulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice recognizing synonyms ('provided that', 'only if', 'whenever', 'for P it is necessary that Q') and converting them into P ⇒ Q, P ⇔ Q forms. This skill is essential for precise mathematical statements and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples and exercises to check understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: The text uses examples (true/false lists, geometric illustrations) and exercises (decide statements, build truth tables, translate sentences) to reinforce definitions and logical manipulation skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work through the provided exercises to internalize truth tables, the meaning of connectives, and the distinction between statements and open sentences; examples model visualization and translation techniques.
